name: Aztec Glyphs
basis: why: the Mexica carved in stone; how: tablets as a height map, glyphs raised, raking light, pigment in hollows
note: The glyph system is the tradition; carving is the process.

lumenary.blurb: A wall of carved stone tablets in the Mexica manner: a square plate for every glyph, the spiral of the wind, the sun, the flint, the serpent, still holding a trace of pigment. Brighter parts of your picture stand higher out of the stone.

facts.bestOn: Pictures with strong light and dark, which raise and lower the relief

why: The Mexica carved in stone, and the best known piece is the Sun Stone, a disc whose rings hold the twenty signs for the days of the ritual count. Twenty signs run against thirteen numbers to give the 260 days of the sacred year. Brighter places in your picture stand higher out of the stone here, and a raking light gives each glyph a shadow.
how: Make a wall of square tablets, each with a raised plate, a raised border and one of eleven glyphs: the spiral of wind, the five-dot movement sign, the stepped fret, the sun, the serpent, the flower, water, the flint, the house, the face and an eight-pointed star.
Set the height of the plate to 0.18 + 0.4 t where t is the picture’s brightness, with the border adding 0.22 and the glyph 0.42.
Paint the heights on a hidden grey canvas, blur it by about a pixel and light it as a relief, from the slope of the surface.
Choose the light direction in degrees, and the stone: basalt, sandstone or limestone.
Add traces of pigment and weathering that gather in the hollows.
history: The Sun Stone, often called the Aztec calendar, was found in Mexico City in 1790. The 260-day count, the tonalpohualli, combined twenty day signs with thirteen numbers. Mexica carvers decorated temples, altars and sculpture, and the glyphs are still studied by archaeologists and honoured by Nahua communities today.
uses: Games and illustration with Mesoamerican themes, made with care
terms: The people commonly called the Aztecs, who built Tenochtitlan.
Light that strikes a surface at a low angle and brings out relief.
paragraphs: The Mexica carved in stone, and the best known piece is the Sun Stone, a disc whose rings hold the twenty signs for the days of the ritual count. Twenty signs run against thirteen numbers to give the 260 days of the sacred year. The program makes a wall of square tablets, each with a raised plate, a raised border and one of eleven glyphs (the spiral of wind, the five-dot movement sign, the stepped fret, the sun, the serpent, the flower, water, the flint, the house, the face and an eight-pointed star), drawn with strokes of different widths. The plate is higher where your picture is brighter: its height is 0.18 + 0.4 t, the border adds 0.22 and the glyph 0.42.

The heights are painted on a hidden grey canvas, blurred by about a pixel, and lit as a relief. The slope of the surface is found from differences of height. Light from the chosen direction brightens the faces that look toward it. Cracks and corners are darkened by an occlusion term, which is large where the surface is lower than its own blur. A wash of the picture’s colours is mixed into the stone, and the glyphs carry stronger paint, because the Mexica painted their stone. Weathering adds long streaks and patches of lichen.

equations.note: The height map: ρ is the depth slider, h_canvas the drawn heights and L̄ a broad blur of the picture’s brightness, which gives the whole wall a gentle swell.
Relief lighting: l = (cos α, sin α) is the direction to the light and k = 22 + 70 ρ scales the slope.
Occlusion: where the height H is below its own blur H̄ (a groove) the surface is darkened by up to 55%.

presets.text: A low light from the side makes the relief deepest.
Heavy pigment recalls a painted temple.
Strong weathering gives an ancient wall.
